title: Jira vs Plane
comparison_markdown:
# Jira vs Plane (2026)

## Overview
Jira and Plane are two project management tools that help teams organize and track their work. This comparison is useful for teams currently using Jira who are considering switching to Plane, possibly due to the core use case of issue tracking and project management. The key reason someone would switch is to take advantage of Plane's self-hosted, free option.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Jira charges per user, while Plane is free for self-hosted deployments.
* Data ownership: Plane allows full control over data as it is self-hosted, whereas Jira stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Plane requires more technical setup, whereas Jira offers a simpler, cloud-based setup.
* Scalability: Jira is designed for large-scale deployments, while Plane's scalability depends on the server infrastructure.
* Integration difference: Jira has a wider range of integrations with third-party tools, while Plane has a more limited set of integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Jira | Plane |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.75-$14.50/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $387.50-$725/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,550-$2,900/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Jira:**
* Wide range of integrations with third-party tools
* Simple, cloud-based setup
* Designed for large-scale deployments
* Robust feature set
* Good customer support
**Plane:**
* Free for self-hosted deployments
* Full control over data
* Highly customizable
* Open-source community
* Limited costs for small teams

## When to Choose Each
Jira is a good choice for large teams that require a wide range of integrations and a simple, cloud-based setup. It is also suitable for teams that need a robust feature set and good customer support. Plane, on the other hand, is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams that want full control over their data and are looking for a free, self-hosted solution. It is also suitable for teams with technical expertise that can handle the more complex setup.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Jira data in CSV or JSON format.
2. Set up a Plane server and configure it according to your needs.
3. Use the Plane import tool to import your Jira data.
4. Configure any necessary integrations and customize Plane to fit your team's workflow.
5. Test the migration to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Plane is not yet production-ready for most users due to its limited scalability and lack of support for large-scale deployments. One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching is that Plane's self-hosted deployment requires a significant amount of technical expertise to set up and maintain. However, for small to medium-sized teams with simple project management needs, Plane is a good choice due to its free, self-hosted option and high customizability.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that do not need a wide range of integrations
* Teams with technical expertise that can handle the complex setup
* Teams that want full control over their data and are looking for a free solution
* Teams with simple project management needs that do not require a robust feature set
* Teams that are currently using Jira's free plan and want to switch to a free, self-hosted solution

## FAQ
### Is Plane free?
Yes, Plane is free for self-hosted deployments.
### Can I integrate Plane with other tools?
Yes, Plane has a limited set of integrations with third-party tools, but it is not as extensive as Jira's.
### Is Plane suitable for large teams?
No, Plane is not yet suitable for large teams due to its limited scalability.
### Can I migrate my Jira data to Plane?
Yes, you can export your Jira data in CSV or JSON format and import it into Plane using the Plane import tool.
### Is Plane open-source?
Yes, Plane is open-source and licensed under the Apache 2.0 license.

title: Trello vs WeKan
comparison_markdown:
# Trello vs WeKan

## Overview

Trello is a visual kanban board tool from Atlassian, simple and beginner-friendly. WeKan is an open-source kanban board offering the same card/list/board model without vendor dependency.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Trello paid plans start at $5/user/month; WeKan is completely free
- **Data control**: WeKan runs on your own server; Trello data lives on Atlassian infrastructure
- **Features**: Trello has a larger Power-Ups marketplace; WeKan covers core kanban features
- **Setup**: Trello requires zero setup; WeKan requires a server
- **Customization**: WeKan open-source code can be extended; Trello cannot

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Trello | WeKan |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $5+/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Trello

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### WeKan

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [wekan/wekan](https://github.com/wekan/wekan) * ~20k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Trello if:** Trello suits individuals and small teams wanting instant zero-setup kanban with integrations to Slack, Google Drive, and GitHub.

**Choose WeKan if:** WeKan is ideal for teams wanting full data ownership or air-gapped deployments.

## Migration Path

Export Trello boards as JSON, then use WeKan Trello importer in Settings to recreate boards, lists, and cards.

## Our Take

WeKan is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Trello tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your WeKan instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Trello, switching to self-hosted WeKan will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Trello until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Trello paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is WeKan free to use?
Yes. WeKan is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Trello to WeKan?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Trello data, follow the WeKan import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does WeKan get regular updates?
Yes. WeKan has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use WeKan without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if WeKan development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced July 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Trello](https://trello.com) and [WeKan](https://wekan.github.io) before making decisions.*

title: Dropbox vs Nextcloud
comparison_markdown:
# Dropbox vs Nextcloud (2026)

## Overview
Dropbox and Nextcloud are two popular cloud storage solutions that enable users to store, share, and collaborate on files. This comparison is beneficial for individuals and teams looking to switch from a proprietary cloud storage service to a self-hosted solution, with the core use case being secure and flexible file management. The key reason someone would switch is to gain control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Dropbox charges a monthly fee per user, while Nextcloud is free to use with self-hosting.
* Data ownership: Nextcloud allows users to retain full ownership of their data, whereas Dropbox's terms of service grant the company certain rights to user data.
* Setup complexity: Nextcloud requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain, especially for self-hosting, compared to Dropbox's straightforward sign-up process.
* Scalability: Nextcloud can be more scalable than Dropbox, especially for large teams or organizations with specific needs, as it can be self-hosted on custom infrastructure.
* Integration with onlyOffice: Nextcloud has a built-in integration with onlyOffice for document editing, whereas Dropbox relies on third-party integrations for similar functionality.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Dropbox | Nextcloud |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $9.99-$16.58/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $499.50-$829/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,998-$3,316/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Dropbox:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Wide range of third-party integrations
* Robust security features
* Good customer support
* Limited control over data storage and management
**Nextcloud:**
* Self-hosting option for full data control
* High scalability and customization
* Integrated document editing with onlyOffice
* Free to use with self-hosting
* Requires technical expertise for setup and maintenance
* Limited user interface customization options

## When to Choose Each
Dropbox is suitable for small to medium-sized teams that prioritize ease of use and don't require full control over their data. It's ideal for teams that already use a range of third-party tools and want to integrate them with their cloud storage. Nextcloud, on the other hand, is better suited for larger teams or organizations that require high scalability, customization, and control over their data. It's also a good choice for teams with in-house technical expertise who can handle the setup and maintenance.

## Migration Path
1. Export your files from Dropbox in ZIP format.
2. Set up a Nextcloud instance on your server or use a pre-configured appliance.
3. Use the Nextcloud web interface to import your files from the ZIP archive.
4. Configure any necessary settings, such as user accounts and permissions.
5. Test your Nextcloud instance to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Nextcloud is a production-ready solution for most users, offering a high degree of customization and control over data. However, it's essential to be aware of the technical limitations, such as the need for in-house expertise for setup and maintenance. We recommend switching to Nextcloud for teams that require high scalability and control over their data, while smaller teams may find Dropbox's ease of use and third-party integrations more suitable.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams with high data security requirements and fewer than 10 users who don't need advanced collaboration features
* Medium-sized teams with 10-50 users who require custom integration with other tools and don't need phone support
* Large teams with 50-200 users who need high scalability and control over their data and don't require a user-friendly interface
* Teams with in-house technical expertise who can handle setup and maintenance and don't need advanced customer support
* Organizations with strict data storage and management regulations who don't need advanced collaboration features

## FAQ
### Can I use Nextcloud for free?
Yes, Nextcloud is free to use with self-hosting, but you'll need to cover the costs of hosting and maintaining your server.
### Is Nextcloud more secure than Dropbox?
Nextcloud offers a high degree of security and control over data, but the actual security depends on the setup and configuration of your instance.
### Can I integrate Nextcloud with other tools?
Yes, Nextcloud has a range of integrations with third-party tools, including onlyOffice for document editing.
### Is Dropbox better for small teams?
Yes, Dropbox is often a better choice for small teams that prioritize ease of use and don't require full control over their data.
### Can I migrate my files from Dropbox to Nextcloud automatically?
Not yet, but you can export your files from Dropbox and import them into Nextcloud using the web interface.
meta_description: Nextcloud, a free self-hosted cloud storage solution, offers high scalability and customization. See full comparison or Free migration guide.

# Microsoft Teams vs Mattermost (2026)

## Overview
Microsoft Teams and Mattermost are two popular team collaboration platforms that offer a range of features to enhance communication and productivity. Both tools are designed for teams and organizations looking to streamline their workflow, with the core use case being real-time messaging, file sharing, and integrations. The key reason someone would switch from Microsoft Teams to Mattermost is to gain more control over their data and hosting, as well as to take advantage of Mattermost's self-hosted option.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Microsoft Teams offers a free version, as well as paid plans starting at $6 per user per month, while Mattermost is free and open-source, with optional paid support.
* Data ownership: Mattermost allows teams to self-host their instance, giving them full control over their data, while Microsoft Teams stores data on its own servers.
* Setup complexity: Microsoft Teams is generally easier to set up, with a more streamlined onboarding process, while Mattermost requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* Scalability: Both platforms are highly scalable, but Mattermost's self-hosted option gives teams more flexibility to customize their infrastructure.
* Integration difference: Microsoft Teams has native integration with Microsoft Office 365 tools, while Mattermost has a more extensive library of third-party integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Microsoft Teams | Mattermost |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $6-$22/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT / AGPL |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $300-$1,100/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,200-$4,400/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Microsoft Teams:**
* Easy to set up and use
* Native integration with Microsoft Office 365 tools
* Large user community and support resources
* Free version available
* Limited customization options

title: Google Workspace vs Nextcloud
comparison_markdown:
# Google Workspace vs Nextcloud

## Overview

Google suite of cloud productivity tools including Gmail, Drive, Docs, Sheets, Meet, and Calendar. is a popular proprietary tool in the productivity space. Nextcloud is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Google Workspace costs $6-$18/user/month; Nextcloud is Free (self-hosted)
- **License**: Google Workspace is Proprietary; Nextcloud is AGPL 3.0
- **Data ownership**: Nextcloud can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Nextcloud eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Nextcloud has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Google Workspace | Nextcloud |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | $6-$18/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | ~$300/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | ~$1,200/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Google Workspace

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Nextcloud

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [nextcloud/server](https://github.com/nextcloud/server) * ~27k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Google Workspace if:** Google Workspace is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Nextcloud if:** Nextcloud is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Google Workspace in its standard export format, review Nextcloud import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Nextcloud is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Google Workspace tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Nextcloud instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Google Workspace, switching to self-hosted Nextcloud will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Google Workspace until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Google Workspace paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Nextcloud free to use?
Yes. Nextcloud is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Google Workspace to Nextcloud?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Google Workspace data, follow the Nextcloud import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Nextcloud get regular updates?
Yes. Nextcloud has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Nextcloud without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Nextcloud development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced July 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Google Workspace](https://workspace.google.com) and [Nextcloud](https://nextcloud.com) before making decisions.*
